expectedText:
HEALTH CARE WORKER WHISTLEBLOWER PROTECTION (HEALTH & SAFETY CODE §1278.5) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme, Inc.

ABOUT THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet describes California Health and Safety Code section 1278.5, a whistleblower-protection statute specific to health facilities. It covers the statute's protection for patients, employees, members of the medical staff, and other health care workers who report or participate in an investigation of suspected unsafe patient care, services, or conditions at a health facility such as Acme, Inc., along with the rebuttable presumptions, penalties, and remedies the statute creates. It is distinct from this corpus's separate information sheet on Labor Code section 1102.5, California's general whistleblower-protection statute, which is not limited to patient-care or health-facility issues and does not contain this statute's health-facility-specific presumptions, remedies, or peer-review provisions. This document explains what the statute states; it is not a substitute for consulting a licensed attorney about a specific set of facts.

LEGISLATIVE PURPOSE, AND WHAT THIS STATUTE IS NOT
California has declared it the state's public policy to encourage patients, nurses, members of the medical staff, and other health care workers to notify government entities of suspected unsafe patient care and conditions, in order to protect patients and to assist the accreditation and government entities responsible for ensuring that health care is safe. The Legislature has separately stated that this statute's whistleblower protections apply primarily to issues relating to the care, services, and conditions of a facility, and are not intended to conflict with existing state and federal law governing the employee-employer relationship generally.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "it is the public policy of the State of California to encourage patients, nurses, members of the medical staff, and other health care workers to notify government entities of suspected unsafe patient care and conditions"
  — Cal. Health & Saf. Code § 1278.5 (California Legislative Information text), California Health and Safety Code § 1278.5(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=HSC&sectionNum=1278.5.)
  "whistleblower protections apply primarily to issues relating to the care, services, and conditions of a facility and are not intended to conflict with existing provisions in state and federal law relating to employee and employer relations"
  — Cal. Health & Saf. Code § 1278.5 (California Legislative Information text), California Health and Safety Code § 1278.5(a) (same subdivision as the preceding citation, not an independent source) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=HSC&sectionNum=1278.5.)
  Known gap: Both quotations in this clause are drawn from the same subdivision of the same statutory section, Health & Safety Code § 1278.5(a), not from independent sources. This clause states the Legislature's own description of the statute's purpose and intended scope; it does not resolve, for any particular report, whether that report actually concerns patient care, services, or facility conditions as opposed to a general employment matter that this statute's findings say it does not intend to reach.

WHAT A HEALTH FACILITY, OR ITS OWNER/OPERATOR, MAY NOT DO
A health facility may not discriminate or retaliate, in any manner, against a patient, employee, member of the medical staff, or other health care worker of the facility because that person presented a grievance, complaint, or report to the facility, to an entity or agency responsible for accrediting or evaluating the facility or its medical staff, or to any other governmental entity, or because that person initiated, participated, or cooperated in an investigation or administrative proceeding related to the quality of care, services, or conditions at the facility that is carried out by such an accrediting or evaluating entity or agency, or by a governmental entity. Separately, an entity that owns or operates the health facility -- or that owns or operates any other health facility -- may not discriminate or retaliate against a person for having taken these same protected actions.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "A health facility shall not discriminate or retaliate, in any manner, against a patient, employee, member of the medical staff, or other health care worker of the health facility because that person has done either of the following:(A) Presented a grievance, complaint, or report to the facility, to an entity or agency responsible for accrediting or evaluating the facility, or the medical staff of the facility, or to any other governmental entity.(B) Has initiated, participated, or cooperated in an investigation or administrative proceeding related to the quality of care, services, or conditions at the facility that is carried out by an entity or agency responsible for accrediting or evaluating the facility or its medical staff, or governmental entity."
  — Cal. Health & Saf. Code § 1278.5 (California Legislative Information text), California Health and Safety Code § 1278.5(b)(1), including subparagraphs (A) and (B) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=HSC&sectionNum=1278.5.)
  "An entity that owns or operates a health facility, or that owns or operates any other health facility, shall not discriminate or retaliate against a person because that person has taken any actions pursuant to this subdivision."
  — Cal. Health & Saf. Code § 1278.5 (California Legislative Information text), California Health and Safety Code § 1278.5(b)(2) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=HSC&sectionNum=1278.5.)
  Known gap: The first citation in this clause spans subdivision (b)(1)'s introductory clause together with both of its listed categories of protected activity, paragraphs (A) and (B), quoted as one contiguous passage from the statute; the second citation is to a separate subdivision, (b)(2), addressing facility owners/operators rather than the facility itself. Both are from the same statutory section and are disclosed together rather than as independent sources. This clause does not itself determine whether any particular report, investigation, or proceeding falls within the statute's description of protected activity.

CIVIL PENALTY FOR A VIOLATION
A violation of this statute is subject to a civil penalty of not more than $25,000. That penalty is assessed and recovered through the same administrative process the statute establishes, at Health and Safety Code Chapter 2.4 beginning at section 1417, for long-term health care facilities.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "A violation of this section shall be subject to a civil penalty of not more than twenty-five thousand dollars ($25,000). The civil penalty shall be assessed and recovered through the same administrative process set forth in Chapter 2.4 (commencing with Section 1417) for long-term health care facilities."
  — Cal. Health & Saf. Code § 1278.5 (California Legislative Information text), California Health and Safety Code § 1278.5(b)(3) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=HSC&sectionNum=1278.5.)
  Known gap: This clause quotes only Health & Safety Code § 1278.5(b)(3); it does not independently fetch or verify the cross-referenced administrative process at Chapter 2.4 (commencing with Section 1417), and does not resolve how that long-term-care-facility administrative process applies procedurally to a violation involving a facility that is not itself a long-term health care facility (a separate subdivision of this same section excludes long-term health care facilities from this statute's substantive coverage; see the coverage-and-exemptions clause of this document).

REBUTTABLE PRESUMPTION PROTECTING A PATIENT
If a patient -- or someone acting on a patient's behalf -- has submitted a grievance or complaint, directly or indirectly, to a governmental entity, or that grievance or complaint has been received by a health facility administrator, and any type of discriminatory treatment of that patient occurs within 180 days of the filing, a rebuttable presumption arises that the facility took the discriminatory action in retaliation for the filing.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Any type of discriminatory treatment of a patient by whom, or upon whose behalf, a grievance or complaint has been submitted, directly or indirectly, to a governmental entity or received by a health facility administrator within 180 days of the filing of the grievance or complaint, shall raise a rebuttable presumption that the action was taken by the health facility in retaliation for the filing of the grievance or complaint."
  — Cal. Health & Saf. Code § 1278.5 (California Legislative Information text), California Health and Safety Code § 1278.5(c) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=HSC&sectionNum=1278.5.)
  Known gap: This clause quotes only Health & Safety Code § 1278.5(c). A related clause of this document addresses the separate 120-day rebuttable presumption that subdivision (d) creates for employees, medical staff, and other health care workers, and the statute's own note (subdivision (e), quoted in that clause) that both presumptions affect only the burden of producing evidence under Evidence Code section 603, which this document does not independently fetch or verify. This clause does not determine, for a specific instance of treatment, whether it in fact qualifies as 'discriminatory treatment' within the 180-day window.

REBUTTABLE PRESUMPTION PROTECTING AN EMPLOYEE, MEDICAL STAFF MEMBER, OR HEALTH CARE WORKER
A separate rebuttable presumption arises for an employee, member of the medical staff, or other health care worker of the facility: if responsible staff at the facility (or the entity that owns or operates it) had knowledge of that person's protected report, participation, or cooperation, and discriminatory action occurs within 120 days of the filing of the grievance or complaint, a rebuttable presumption arises that the facility (or owning/operating entity) retaliated. For this purpose, the statute defines 'discriminatory treatment' to include, without limitation, discharge, demotion, suspension, or any unfavorable change in or breach of the terms or conditions of a contract, employment, or privileges -- or the threat of any of those actions. Both this presumption and the separate one protecting patients are, by the statute's own terms, presumptions that affect only the burden of producing evidence, as provided in Evidence Code section 603.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "There shall be a rebuttable presumption that discriminatory action was taken by the health facility, or by the entity that owns or operates that health facility, or that owns or operates any other health facility, in retaliation against an employee, member of the medical staff, or any other health care worker of the facility, if responsible staff at the facility or the entity that owns or operates the facility had knowledge of the actions, participation, or cooperation of the person responsible for any acts described in paragraph (1) of subdivision (b), and the discriminatory action occurs within 120 days of the filing of the grievance or complaint by the employee, member of the medical staff or any other health care worker of the facility."
  — Cal. Health & Saf. Code § 1278.5 (California Legislative Information text), California Health and Safety Code § 1278.5(d)(1) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=HSC&sectionNum=1278.5.)
  "discriminatory treatment of an employee, member of the medical staff, or any other health care worker includes, but is not limited to, discharge, demotion, suspension, or any unfavorable changes in, or breach of, the terms or conditions of a contract, employment, or privileges of the employee, member of the medical staff, or any other health care worker of the health care facility, or the threat of any of these actions."
  — Cal. Health & Saf. Code § 1278.5 (California Legislative Information text), California Health and Safety Code § 1278.5(d)(2) (same section as the preceding citation, a different subdivision) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=HSC&sectionNum=1278.5.)
  "The presumptions in subdivisions (c) and (d) shall be presumptions affecting the burden of producing evidence as provided in Section 603 of the Evidence Code."
  — Cal. Health & Saf. Code § 1278.5 (California Legislative Information text), California Health and Safety Code § 1278.5(e) (same section as the preceding citations, a different subdivision) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=HSC&sectionNum=1278.5.)
  Known gap: This clause's three citations are to different subdivisions of the same statutory section -- § 1278.5(d)(1), (d)(2), and (e) -- disclosed here rather than presented as independent sources. This document does not independently fetch or verify the text of Evidence Code § 603, which the statute cross-references for the legal effect of a 'presumption affecting the burden of producing evidence.' This clause does not determine, for particular facts, whether the 120-day window or knowledge requirement is satisfied.

CRIMINAL MISDEMEANOR FOR A WILLFUL VIOLATION
A person who willfully violates this statute is guilty of a misdemeanor, punishable by a fine of not more than $75,000, in addition to the civil penalty the statute separately authorizes.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "A person who willfully violates this section is guilty of a misdemeanor punishable by a fine of not more than seventy-five thousand dollars ($75,000), in addition to the civil penalty provided in paragraph (3) of subdivision (b)."
  — Cal. Health & Saf. Code § 1278.5 (California Legislative Information text), California Health and Safety Code § 1278.5(f) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=HSC&sectionNum=1278.5.)
  Known gap: This clause quotes only Health & Safety Code § 1278.5(f). The statute's text does not itself further define 'willfully' for this purpose, and this clause does not determine, for particular facts, whether a violation was willful.

REMEDIES, WHICH DIFFER BY ROLE
The statute provides different remedies depending on the reporting person's relationship to the facility. An employee who has been discriminated against in employment is entitled to reinstatement, reimbursement for lost wages and work benefits caused by the employer's acts, and legal costs of pursuing the case, or to any other remedy the court deems warranted under this chapter or other applicable statutory or common law. A health care worker who is not necessarily an employee (for example, an independent contractor) is entitled to reimbursement for lost income and legal costs, or to any other remedy the court deems warranted, but the statute does not list reinstatement among that person's remedies. A member of the medical staff is entitled to reinstatement, reimbursement for lost income resulting from a change in the terms or conditions of the member's privileges, and legal costs, or to any other remedy the court deems warranted. Separately, the statute states that it does not abrogate or limit any other theory of liability or remedy otherwise available at law.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "An employee who has been discriminated against in employment pursuant to this section shall be entitled to reinstatement, reimbursement for lost wages and work benefits caused by the acts of the employer, and the legal costs associated with pursuing the case, or to any remedy deemed warranted by the court pursuant to this chapter or any other applicable provision of statutory or common law."
  — Cal. Health & Saf. Code § 1278.5 (California Legislative Information text), California Health and Safety Code § 1278.5(g), first sentence (employee remedies) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=HSC&sectionNum=1278.5.)
  "A health care worker who has been discriminated against pursuant to this section shall be entitled to reimbursement for lost income and the legal costs associated with pursuing the case, or to any remedy deemed warranted by the court pursuant to this chapter or other applicable provision of statutory or common law."
  — Cal. Health & Saf. Code § 1278.5 (California Legislative Information text), California Health and Safety Code § 1278.5(g), second sentence (health care worker remedies) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=HSC&sectionNum=1278.5.)
  "A member of the medical staff who has been discriminated against pursuant to this section shall be entitled to reinstatement, reimbursement for lost income resulting from any change in the terms or conditions of the member’s privileges caused by the acts of the facility or the entity that owns or operates a health facility or any other health facility that is owned or operated by that entity, and the legal costs associated with pursuing the case, or to any remedy deemed warranted by the court pursuant to this chapter or any other applicable provision of statutory or common law."
  — Cal. Health & Saf. Code § 1278.5 (California Legislative Information text), California Health and Safety Code § 1278.5(g), third sentence (medical staff member remedies) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=HSC&sectionNum=1278.5.)
  "This section does not abrogate or limit any other theory of liability or remedy otherwise available at law."
  — Cal. Health & Saf. Code § 1278.5 (California Legislative Information text), California Health and Safety Code § 1278.5(m) (same section as the preceding citations, a different subdivision) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=HSC&sectionNum=1278.5.)
  Known gap: This clause's four citations are to different subdivisions of the same statutory section -- § 1278.5(g) (three separate sentences, each addressing a different category of person) and § 1278.5(m) -- disclosed here rather than as independent sources. This clause does not determine which of the statute's three role-based remedy categories applies to a specific reader, nor does it identify what other statutory or common-law theories of liability subdivision (m) preserves.

HOW THIS STATUTE INTERACTS WITH MEDICAL STAFF PEER REVIEW
This statute does not limit the medical staff's ability to carry out its legitimate peer review activities under Business and Professions Code sections 809 to 809.5. It separately allows the medical staff to petition a court for an injunction protecting a peer review committee from evidentiary demands, in a pending peer review hearing, made by a medical staff member who has filed an action under this statute, if those evidentiary demands would impede the peer review process or endanger patient health and safety during that process; before granting an injunction, the court must conduct an in camera review of the evidence sought to determine whether a peer review hearing authorized under Business and Professions Code sections 805 and 809 through 809.5 would be impeded.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "The medical staff of the health facility may petition the court for an injunction to protect a peer review committee from being required to comply with evidentiary demands on a pending peer review hearing from the member of the medical staff who has filed an action pursuant to this section, if the evidentiary demands from the complainant would impede the peer review process or endanger the health and safety of patients of the health facility during the peer review process."
  — Cal. Health & Saf. Code § 1278.5 (California Legislative Information text), California Health and Safety Code § 1278.5(h) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=HSC&sectionNum=1278.5.)
  "This section does not limit the ability of the medical staff to carry out its legitimate peer review activities in accordance with Sections 809 to 809.5, inclusive, of the Business and Professions Code."
  — Cal. Health & Saf. Code § 1278.5 (California Legislative Information text), California Health and Safety Code § 1278.5(l) (same section as the preceding citation, a different subdivision) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=HSC&sectionNum=1278.5.)
  Known gap: This clause's two citations are to different subdivisions of the same statutory section -- § 1278.5(h) and (l) -- disclosed here rather than as independent sources. This document does not independently fetch or verify the cross-referenced Business and Professions Code sections 805 and 809 through 809.5, which govern the peer review process itself.

WHAT COUNTS AS A "HEALTH FACILITY," AND WHO THIS STATUTE DOES NOT COVER
For purposes of this statute, a "health facility" means a facility defined under the same chapter of the Health and Safety Code, including, without limitation, the facility's administrative personnel, employees, boards and board committees, and medical staff. This statute does not apply to an inmate of a correctional facility or juvenile facility of the Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation, or to an inmate housed in a local detention facility such as a county jail, juvenile hall, or juvenile camp. It also does not apply to a health facility that is a long-term health care facility, as separately defined at Health and Safety Code section 1418 -- a long-term health care facility instead remains subject to Health and Safety Code section 1432.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "For purposes of this section, “health facility” means a facility defined under this chapter, including, but not limited to, the facility’s administrative personnel, employees, boards, and committees of the board, and medical staff."
  — Cal. Health & Saf. Code § 1278.5 (California Legislative Information text), California Health and Safety Code § 1278.5(i) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=HSC&sectionNum=1278.5.)
  "This section does not apply to an inmate of a correctional facility or juvenile facility of the Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation, or to an inmate housed in a local detention facility including a county jail or a juvenile hall, juvenile camp, or other juvenile detention facility."
  — Cal. Health & Saf. Code § 1278.5 (California Legislative Information text), California Health and Safety Code § 1278.5(j) (same section as the preceding citation, a different subdivision) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=HSC&sectionNum=1278.5.)
  "This section does not apply to a health facility that is a long-term health care facility, as defined in Section 1418. A health facility that is a long-term health care facility shall remain subject to Section 1432."
  — Cal. Health & Saf. Code § 1278.5 (California Legislative Information text), California Health and Safety Code § 1278.5(k) (same section as the preceding citations, a different subdivision) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=HSC&sectionNum=1278.5.)
  Known gap: This clause's three citations are to different subdivisions of the same statutory section -- § 1278.5(i), (j), and (k) -- disclosed here rather than as independent sources. This document does not independently fetch or verify the definition of "health facility" in the chapter this subdivision cross-references (Health and Safety Code Chapter 2 of Division 2, which includes section 1250), nor the separate long-term-care-facility statutes it names, sections 1418 and 1432, so no claim is made here about their content.

RIGHT TO SPEAK PRIVATELY WITH A HEALTH FACILITY INSPECTOR
An employee, or the employee's representative, has the right to discuss possible regulatory violations or patient safety concerns with the inspector privately, during the course of an investigation or inspection carried out by the department.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "An employee or the employee’s representative shall have the right to discuss possible regulatory violations or patient safety concerns with the inspector privately during the course of an investigation or inspection by the department."
  — Cal. Health & Saf. Code § 1278.5 (California Legislative Information text), California Health and Safety Code § 1278.5(n) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=HSC&sectionNum=1278.5.)
  Known gap: This clause quotes only Health & Safety Code § 1278.5(n). The statute's text does not itself define which "department" conducts the referenced investigation or inspection in every context, and this document does not independently research that definition beyond the statutory text quoted here.

ACKNOWLEDGMENT
Please sign below to acknowledge that you have received and read this document.

Employee: Jordan Lee
Health facility / company: Acme, Inc.
Date: September 1, 2026
City, State: Oakland, California

expectedJSON.body: The statute provides different remedies depending on the reporting person's relationship to the facility. An employee who has been discriminated against in employment is entitled to reinstatement, reimbursement for lost wages and work benefits caused by the employer's acts, and legal costs of pursuing the case, or to any other remedy the court deems warranted under this chapter or other applicable statutory or common law. A health care worker who is not necessarily an employee (for example, an independent contractor) is entitled to reimbursement for lost income and legal costs, or to any other remedy the court deems warranted, but the statute does not list reinstatement among that person's remedies. A member of the medical staff is entitled to reinstatement, reimbursement for lost income resulting from a change in the terms or conditions of the member's privileges, and legal costs, or to any other remedy the court deems warranted. Separately, the statute states that it does not abrogate or limit any other theory of liability or remedy otherwise available at law.

expectedJSON.body: This statute does not limit the medical staff's ability to carry out its legitimate peer review activities under Business and Professions Code sections 809 to 809.5. It separately allows the medical staff to petition a court for an injunction protecting a peer review committee from evidentiary demands, in a pending peer review hearing, made by a medical staff member who has filed an action under this statute, if those evidentiary demands would impede the peer review process or endanger patient health and safety during that process; before granting an injunction, the court must conduct an in camera review of the evidence sought to determine whether a peer review hearing authorized under Business and Professions Code sections 805 and 809 through 809.5 would be impeded.

expectedJSON.body: For purposes of this statute, a "health facility" means a facility defined under the same chapter of the Health and Safety Code, including, without limitation, the facility's administrative personnel, employees, boards and board committees, and medical staff. This statute does not apply to an inmate of a correctional facility or juvenile facility of the Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation, or to an inmate housed in a local detention facility such as a county jail, juvenile hall, or juvenile camp. It also does not apply to a health facility that is a long-term health care facility, as separately defined at Health and Safety Code section 1418 -- a long-term health care facility instead remains subject to Health and Safety Code section 1432.
